comment: The version sweep. versions.json compares two points — the release JBrowse 2
pinned in 2023 against the current one — which says how much faster the
parsers got but not where the change landed. This file names every major
line in between so the answer can be a curve rather than a ratio.
Selection rule: the newest patch of each major line, read off npm on
2026-08-16. Newest-patch rather than first-release of each major because a
major line accumulates fixes after its .0, and the last patch is the one that
line finally became; the first .0 would credit the next major with work its
predecessor shipped.
The rule has one consequence worth stating rather than discovering: the 2023
pins in versions.json are NOT sweep points. @gmod/bam v2.0.0 is the pin and
v2.0.4 is the sweep's major-2 point. They are close but not identical, so a
sweep row and a versions.json row for the same major are two measurements,
not one repeated. sweep.ts marks the major each 2023 pin falls inside.
A version that will not build from source with today's toolchain is recorded
as unbuildable and skipped, not fatal — setup.sh --sweep keeps going. Which
of a library's majors can still be built at all is itself a result, so it is
reported rather than silently dropped.
vcf-js and bgzf-filehandle are here too, but they get a curve and no
request-shape column: neither takes a filehandle the way the other three
do. @gmod/vcf is handed lines that a reader already decoded, and
bgzf-filehandle is handed a buffer. So MODE=count reports nothing for them
and their rows are timings, which means they need an idle box where the
other three do not.
rule: newest patch of each major line, npm as of 2026-08-16

libraries.name: cram-js
comment: v1 through v3 import generic-filehandle without declaring it, the same
defect versions.json records as extraDeps for v1.7.1 and for the same
reason: npm's flat node_modules hoisted it out of a transitive dep and
pnpm does not hoist. ^3.0.0 is the range jbrowse-components pinned at
the time. v3.0.7 needs it too, which only showed up when the arm failed
to import — the build succeeds either way.
Every major before 8 defaults fetchSizeLimit to 3 MB and throws past it,
which every long-read window in this corpus exceeds. JBrowse 2 never ran
that default — its CramAdapter set 200_000_000 — so the arm passes the
same value to any version that accepts it. That is the identical
adjustment lib/corpus.ts already documents as OLD_CRAM_OPTS, applied
across the sweep rather than only to the 2023 point.

libraries.name: bbi-js
comment: The single-file BigWig case is 1-3 ms and versions.json reports it as
flat to slightly negative. Read the sweep here for shape, not for a
headline: cohort-bw.ts is where this library's cost becomes legible,
because a per-file fixed cost is what a signal panel pays 100 times.

libraries.name: vcf-js
comment: Measured through parseLine alone, on every version, deliberately. The
two-point benchmark in vcf.bench.ts asks each side for genotypes
through the cheapest call it offers — SAMPLES on v5, GENOTYPES() on
v7 — because that is what a JBrowse upgrade actually buys. A sweep
cannot do that: the API appears partway along the axis, so the curve
would carry a step that is a change of question rather than a change
of speed. parseLine exists on every major and means the same thing on
each, so the curve is one measurement repeated.
Corpus is the VCF one rather than the alignments: what a VCF parser
costs scales with samples x variants, not with read depth.

libraries.name: bgzf-filehandle
comment: The browser path on every version, which means a different export name
on either side of the split. v1.4.3 shipped two decompressors and chose
between them at import time — `unzip` wraps zlib.gunzip in Node, and
browsers got `pakoUnzip` — while later versions have one implementation
everywhere. The arm therefore prefers pakoUnzip and falls back to
unzip, so every point on the curve is the pure-JS path a genome browser
actually runs. Sweeping `unzip` instead would compare C++ against
JavaScript at the version where the split ends and report it as a
regression.
1000x is left out for the reason bgzf.bench.ts leaves it out: BAM is
BGZF end to end, so unzipping it would materialize gigabytes per
iteration and measure the garbage collector.
